title: Similarity by Selected Traits
outcome: By the end, I can calculate a feature distance and state how scaling changes its meaning.
scenario: A fictional toy book matcher represents two preferences with numeric features.
given: Target vector [2,5]. Candidate A=[2,2], B=[4,5], C=[3,4].
Use Manhattan distance: add absolute coordinate differences; return all smallest-distance candidates.

steps.label: Choose closest
steps.detail: B and C tie at distance 2; keep the tie visible.

explanation: Each coordinate contributes according to the declared distance rule. Smaller distance means closer in this representation, not automatically a better reading experience. If one coordinate uses a much larger numerical scale, it can dominate the sum even when it is not more important. Feature units and scaling belong in the method record.

counterfactual.change: Give the first-coordinate difference weight 2 while the second keeps weight 1.
counterfactual.prediction: Distances become A=3, B=4, C=3; A and C tie.
counterfactual.reason: The representation’s comparison rule changes; the supplied vectors stay the same.

student_task: Explain why B ceases to be a closest option without any candidate data changing.
teacher_answer: Its first-coordinate gap 2 now contributes 4, raising its distance above A and C’s 3.
project_evidence: Specify recommender feature meanings, units, scaling and tie policy before explaining nearest matches.
limits: A toy numeric encoding does not establish meaningful interpersonal distances or suitability of a recommendation.
review_note: New fictional case individually matched to this topic, with computations and policy traces checked. Use for supported practice; preserve the independent assessment.

mini_visual.title: Toy feature positions
mini_visual.metric: Manhattan distance; horizontal=first feature, vertical=second feature
